title: Talking to GitHub from code

story: PR #2512 for RH-1234 grew during its review. Nova, our agent that turns a Jira ticket into a pull request, pushes a small checkpoint commit after every step that works, and in the middle a teammate pushed a one-line typo fix, which became commit 31. Nova then answered the review comments with three more commits, and the teammate approved the latest one. That approval should not count: whoever pushed code to a PR is part of the change, so they are not an independent reviewer.

Now suppose the independent-approval check, the required check that looks for one approval from outside the change, reads the PR's commits with one simple call. It goes green. GitHub answered that call with the first 30 commits, because that is the default page size. Commit 31, the only one with the teammate's name on it, was on page two, and nobody asked for page two.
hook.question: How do we read pull requests, reviews and checks from code without missing anything, and how do we know which commit each of them is about?

read.h: One client, one method per endpoint
p: Octokit is GitHub's official JavaScript client for its API. You create one client with a token, and it gives you one method per API endpoint, grouped by area: octokit.rest.pulls.get reads a pull request, octokit.rest.pulls.listReviews lists its reviews, octokit.rest.checks.listForRef lists the check runs of a commit. Every method takes one object with owner, repo and the endpoint's own fields, and returns { data, status, headers }. The types come from GitHub's API description, so your editor completes pr.user.login and pr.head.sha for you.

What a call may do depends only on the token. In a workflow you pass the job's GITHUB_TOKEN, in the broker the one-hour App token, and on your laptop the token of the gh CLI. With a read-only token, pulls.create answers 403 Forbidden, which is correct and is not a bug in your code. Here is the start of the independent-approval check, the required check that passes only when someone other than the requester approved the latest commit.

notes.text: GitHub sets GITHUB_REPOSITORY, for example RhinoHealth/fcp, in every job.
One client per process. It adds the authorization header and the API version to every call.
Take data straight away; status and headers are rarely needed.

read.h: Every list has a page two
p: Lists are where code goes wrong quietly. GitHub never returns a whole list at once: most list endpoints return 30 items unless you ask for more, at most 100 per page, and they put a link to the next page in a response header. One call gives you page one and no error, so the bug in the story looks exactly like a working check until a PR is long enough.

octokit.paginate fixes it. You pass the method itself, not a call to it, plus the parameters, and it follows the next-page links until the end and gives you one array. Use it for every list whose length you do not control: commits, reviews, files, check runs and workflow runs. Ask for per_page: 100 so it needs as few calls as possible.

notes.text: Returns at most 30 commits. On a PR with 34, the last four are simply not there.
paginate takes the method, not its result, and returns every commit in one array.
A commit's GitHub author can be null when git's email matches no account; filter(Boolean) drops those.

deeper.h: Go deeper: GraphQL when you need many nested things
p: The REST API returns one kind of thing per call. For a nightly job that needs 300 PRs, each with its commits and its review timeline, that means thousands of calls. GitHub's GraphQL API lets you ask for exactly the nested fields you need in one request, and it pages with a cursor: you ask for pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor } and pass endCursor back as the after variable.
Octokit includes it as octokit.graphql(query, variables). Our metrics job uses a GraphQL search per week of PRs, because GitHub's search stops at 1,000 results for one query.

read.h: Tie everything to the head commit
p: A pull request moves. Every push gives it a new head, the newest commit of its branch, and the PR object tells you its SHA as pr.head.sha. Reviews and check runs are attached to commits, not to the PR as a whole: each review has a commit_id, the head at the moment it was submitted, and each check run has a head_sha. So 'approved' only means something together with 'which commit'. An approval whose commit_id is an older commit approved code that is no longer what would be merged.

That is why the check keeps the head SHA and compares every review with it, and why it asks for the check runs of that one commit with checks.listForRef. It also keeps only reviews from people (user.type is User), because approvals from bots never count, and that includes Byte, our review agent.

notes.text: The commit that would be merged right now.
An approval counts only if it is for this exact commit and comes from a person.
Check runs belong to a commit, so you ask by ref: the head SHA.
conclusion is null while a check is still running, so it counts as not passing yet.

p: Writing looks like reading. pulls.create takes the base branch, the head branch, a title, a body and draft: true. Agent PRs always open as drafts, and the body always ends with a Requested-by: line, because the PR's author is the bot and the independent-approval check needs to know which person asked for the work. Labels are set through the issues API, because on GitHub every pull request is also an issue with the same number.

In our platform the agent's VM never runs this code with a token. It asks the broker, and the broker makes exactly these calls with its one-hour App token, after checking that the branch and repo belong to the run. Some calls the broker never makes at all, even though its token could: it never merges, never approves and never starts a workflow.

The Requested-by: line is a contract: the independent-approval check reads exactly this line.

lab.title: Read one PR the way the check does
needs: The gh CLI, logged in; its token is only used to read a public repo
lab.goal: Read a real public PR with Octokit, see what one unpaged call misses, tie its reviews and checks to its head commit, and build a draft PR request without sending it.

guess.q: A PR has 40 commits. Your code calls octokit.rest.pulls.listCommits({ owner, repo, pull_number }) once. How many commits does it get back?

options.why: GitHub returns one page per call. Without per_page, the page size is 30.

options.text: 30, the default page size, with no error.
options.why: The rest is on page two, behind a link in the response headers. That silence is what makes the bug dangerous.

options.text: An error, because the list is too long.
options.why: GitHub never fails a long list. It pages it, and it is your job to ask for the next page.

follow.say: Save a teammate's first try at 'is the latest commit approved?' for the Fix it step.

lab.build: Write pr.mjs that reads PR 14640 of cli/cli and prints four things: the head SHA; the number of commits and who wrote them, using octokit.paginate; one line per review with the reviewer, whether it is a User or a Bot, the state, and whether it is on the head or on an older commit; and the check runs on the head commit counted by conclusion (checks.listForRef with ref: the head SHA, and Object.groupBy). Run it with GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) node pr.mjs.
checks: pr.mjs prints commits: 40, the same number as gh pr view.
Two reviews are printed: a Bot that COMMENTED on an older commit, and a User that APPROVED on the head.
The checks line says 7 skipped, 11 success.
Every list in pr.mjs goes through octokit.paginate with per_page: 100.
After Fix it, node fix.mjs says the latest commit is approved.
lab.fix: Run GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) node fix.mjs. It says there is no approval on the latest commit, but your pr.mjs just showed a person approving the head. Find the one wrong property, fix it, and explain in one sentence the difference between the two SHAs it confused.
explain: Why did one call to listCommits return 30 commits without any error, and what does paginate do differently?
Why must a review's commit_id match the PR's head SHA before the approval counts?
In our platform, who actually sends the pulls.create call for Nova, and with which token?
lab.done: pr.mjs prints 40 commits, both reviews with the commit they belong to, and the head's checks, and fix.mjs finds the approval.

check.q: A check counts the people who pushed to a PR with one call to pulls.listCommits. Which PR can fool it?

options.text: A PR whose last commits were pushed by someone new, after the first 30 commits
options.why: One call returns one page, 30 commits by default. Anyone who only appears on page two is invisible.

options.text: A PR with commits from only one person
options.why: If one person wrote every commit, page one already shows them.
Draft or ready makes no difference to how commits are listed.

check.q: A teammate approved PR #2512. Then Nova pushed a new commit. What does the review's commit_id say?

options.text: The new head, because GitHub moves reviews forward with the branch
options.why: Reviews stay on the commit they were given for. Nothing moves them forward.

options.text: The commit that was the head when the teammate approved, which is no longer the head
options.why: That is how the check knows the approval is for older code: commit_id differs from pr.head.sha.
The base is the commit on main the PR is compared against. A review is never attached to it.

check.q: Code with a read-only token calls pulls.create and gets 403 Forbidden. What is wrong?

options.text: Octokit needs a different client for write calls
options.why: The same client does reads and writes. Only the token's permissions differ.

options.text: The body is missing the Requested-by: line
options.why: GitHub knows nothing about that line. It is our own contract with the check.

options.text: Nothing in the code: the token decides what is allowed, and read-only cannot open a PR
options.why: Permissions live in the token, not in the code. A 403 here means the token is doing its job.

p: Three parts of the platform read GitHub with exactly these calls. The independent-approval check reads the PR, all its commits and reviews, and compares each review with the head SHA. The nightly metrics job lists PRs, workflow runs on main and check runs per commit to compute delivery numbers. And the broker opens draft PRs, adds labels and comments for agent runs with its one-hour App token, while refusing merge, approve and dispatch.
Every one of them goes through paginate for lists, because a missed page in a check is a security bug, and a missed page in a metric is a wrong number.

tickets.why: main() of the independent-approval check: reads the PR, commits and reviews with Octokit and sets the exit code.
The nightly metrics job pulls PRs with their timeline through a GraphQL search, one week per query.
Red-main hours come from listing workflow runs on main and the jobs of each run.
firstPassGreen needs the check runs of one commit: checks.listForRef by head SHA.
The broker's small allow-list of GitHub calls: create a draft, mark its own PR ready, comment; never merge.

words.plain: GitHub's official JavaScript client: one typed method per API endpoint, such as octokit.rest.pulls.get.
GitHub returns long lists one page at a time (30 items by default, 100 at most); you must ask for the next pages.
octokit.paginate(method, params): follows every next-page link and returns one array.
The newest commit of the PR's branch, the code that would be merged right now.
One check's result on one commit, with a name, a head_sha and a conclusion.

review.q: Write from memory the line that lists every review of a PR with Octokit.
review.a: const reviews = await octokit.paginate(octokit.rest.pulls.listReviews, { owner, repo, pull_number, per_page: 100 }).

review.q: Which two fields do you compare to decide whether an approval is for the code that would be merged?
review.a: The review's commit_id and the PR's head.sha. They must be equal, and the reviewer must be a person (user.type User).

review.q: Why does Nova's VM not call pulls.create itself?
review.a: The VM holds no GitHub token. It asks the broker, which checks the run's scope and makes the call with its own one-hour App token.

remember: Page through every list with paginate, and judge every review and check by the commit it belongs to: the head SHA.
